input.question: During the age of Caribbean piracy, were there any pirate havens or free cities on the coast?
input.ground_truth: The Bahamas and some of the surrounding area was relatively safe for pirates and their crews (including Port Royal and Tortuga). Colin Woodard covers exactly this and more in his book [*The Republic of Pirates: Being the True and Surprising Story of the Caribbean Pirates and the Man Who Brought Them Down*](_URL_0_). I highly recommend this book. It is very easy to read and follows three pirates and pirate-hunter Woodes Rogers during the golden age of piracy (which Woodard argues as 1715-1725). The only thing that irks me about this book is the way Woodard cites his sources. Instead of using endnotes in the text, he simply lists page numbers and where he got the information in the his bibliography at the back of the book. This is near my period of study, so I may be able to answer more questions depending on what or how specific they are.

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: During the age of Caribbean piracy, were there any pirate havens or free cities on the coast?

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine you have a big playground, and some kids there don’t want to follow the rules. They are called “pirate kids.” Now, in the old days, some special places by the sea were like secret playgrounds for these pirate kids. These places didn’t care if the pirate kids broke the rules. They let them stay and even helped them sometimes!

These special places are called “pirate havens” or “free cities.” For example, there was a place called Nassau, on a big island called New Providence. The pirate kids (real pirates!) would go there to hide, fix their boats, and share their treasure. The grown-ups in charge there didn’t stop them, as long as the pirates were nice to them and didn’t cause too much trouble.

So yes, there were secret places by the sea where pirates could rest and feel safe!
